hops.title: The kitchen stain that works by missing almost everything
hops.text: In 1872 Camillo Golgi took a post at a hospital for the chronically ill in Abbiategrasso, outside Milan, and converted a little kitchen into a laboratory. There, in 1873, he found his silver black reaction, the first method to show a neuron in its entirety, cell body to finest branch. The odd part is that it fills only about 1 to 3 percent of the neurons in a slice. That miss rate is what makes it work. Had the silver darkened every neuron in that tangle at once, the section would read as a black smudge instead of a few legible branching trees.

sources.citation: The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 1906, Camillo Golgi - Biographical, NobelPrize.org.
Pannese, E. (1996). The black reaction. Brain Research Bulletin, 41(6), 343-349. PMID: 8973838.
Zaqout, S., & Kaindl, A. M. (2016). Golgi-Cox staining step by step. Frontiers in Neuroanatomy, 10, 38. PMC4814522.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A brass microscope, glass slides and staining jars on an old wooden kitchen table beside an oil lamp.
image.caption: Golgi's kitchen silver stain showed whole neurons because it left almost every neighbor unstained.

hops.title: Adult canaries add fresh neurons to their song center
hops.text: Adult canaries do not keep only the neurons they hatched with. In 1983 Steven Goldman and Fernando Nottebohm gave adult female canaries tritiated thymidine over two days, then examined their brains about five weeks after hormone implants, asking whether testosterone, which drives male-like singing, added cells to the vocal control center HVc. The share of labeled HVc neurons came out alike in testosterone-treated birds and cholesterol controls, at roughly two to four percent in both groups. Precursor cells in the ventricular zone had copied their DNA during the two-day pulse, and their daughters migrated into HVc, so this adult brain was making neurons even without added testosterone.

sources.citation: Goldman, S. A., & Nottebohm, F. (1983). Neuronal production, migration, and differentiation in a vocal control nucleus of the adult female canary brain. PNAS, 80(8), 2390-2394. PMID: 6572982.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A bright yellow canary perched on a sunlit twig with its beak open as if singing.
image.caption: A two-day thymidine pulse caught adult canaries adding new neurons to their song center.

hops.title: Why the first cloned cat did not match her donor's coat
hops.text: Most people expect a clone to be a photocopy. CC, short for Copy Cat, was born at Texas A&M in December 2001, the first cloned pet, and matching DNA markers confirmed her nuclear DNA came from a domestic shorthair named Rainbow. Her coat did not match. Rainbow was calico, and a calico's orange and dark patches trace to the X-linked orange locus: early embryonic cells randomly silence one X, and pigment-cell precursors inherit and pass on that state, so each patch reflects one lineage's active X. Texas A&M put CC's different coat down to developmental factors. Identical nuclear DNA plainly does not dictate the pattern.

sources.citation: Texas A&M College of Veterinary Medicine. CVM researchers first to clone cat (press release).
Texas A&M College of Veterinary Medicine. Texas A&M says goodbye to CC, world's first cloned cat.
Toh, H., et al. (2025). The X-linked orange locus and random X inactivation in domestic cats. PMID: 40378840.
Shin, T., et al. (2002). A cat cloned by nuclear transplantation. Nature, 415, 859. PMID: 11859353.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A calico cat and a differently patterned cat sitting side by side on a sunny windowsill.
image.caption: CC inherited Rainbow's nuclear DNA and still grew a coat with a different pattern.
